title: From the control room to the turkey farm: Arkansas Nuclear One employee helps bring Thanksgiving to the table
summary: For many families, Thanksgiving wouldn’t be complete without a turkey on the table. For one Arkansas Nuclear One employee, raising those turkeys is a year-round tradition.
body_markdown:
For many families, Thanksgiving wouldn’t be complete without a turkey on the table. For one Arkansas Nuclear One employee, raising those turkeys is a year-round tradition.


Theron Rowbotham has spent the last 20 years working for Entergy Arkansas at Arkansas Nuclear One (ANO). As a Unit 2 Initial License Operator Instructor, he helps train future nuclear plant operators to safely and reliably operate the plant. But when he’s not in the classroom, you’ll find him tending to a different kind of operation.


Rowbotham is a seventh-generation turkey and cattle farmer in Johnson County, Ark., where he runs Infinity Ranch.


“I raise turkeys for Butterball, so the turkeys that you see in the store, wrapped as a whole turkey anywhere from 10 to 15 pounds, that’s what I grow for Butterball,” Rowbotham said.


His facility includes four turkey houses, each holding approximately 16,000 to 17,000 birds. Rowbotham raises the turkeys from the time they hatch until they’re 12 weeks old, helping supply a Thanksgiving staple for families across the country.


While operating a nuclear power plant and raising turkeys may seem worlds apart, Rowbotham says the two have more in common than you might think.


“Here at the turkey farm, we also have a control room,” Rowbotham said. “We control pumps, fans and monitor water pressure and how much feed goes to the turkeys. Now, it may not be as complicated or have as many switches as the ANO control room.”


Both operations require careful monitoring, attention to detail and a commitment to doing things the right way. Still, Rowbotham admits one job has its advantages.


“Turkeys are way easier to work with than ILO students, you know,” he joked.


Whether he’s helping prepare the next generation of nuclear operators or raising turkeys for Thanksgiving dinner, Rowbotham takes pride in the work he does and the impact it has on others.


“What I wish people knew about Entergy was how safe and reliable it really is,” Rowbotham said.


This Thanksgiving, as families gather around the table, Rowbotham’s story is a reminder of the many ways Entergy Arkansas employees serve their communities — both on and off the job.
